CHAPTER 21 — शल्यचिकित्साजनकः सुश्रुतः (SHALYACHIKITSA-JANAKAH SUSHRUTAH)

Introduction — पाठपरिचयः

This lesson presents, in simple Sanskrit prose with English support, the story of सुश्रुतः (Sushruta) — the ancient surgeon of वाराणसी (Varanasi) who is honoured across the world as शल्यचिकित्साजनकः, the 'father of surgery'. We read about his life, his great work the सुश्रुतसंहिता, the surgical instruments (यन्त्र-शस्त्र) he described, famous procedures such as नासासंधानम् (rhinoplasty, reconstruction of the nose), his remarkable training methods for students, the ethics (वैद्यधर्मः) he demanded of physicians, and his global legacy. NOTE: This chapter is a study of the HISTORY of Indian science and of Sanskrit language. It describes ancient practices as history; it is NOT medical advice or instruction of any kind. For any health matter, a qualified modern doctor must be consulted.

संस्कृतपाठः — मूलगद्यम् (Original simple Sanskrit prose)

(१) प्राचीनभारते वाराणसीनगरे सुश्रुतः नाम महान् वैद्यः आसीत्। सः गङ्गायाः तीरे न्यवसत्। सः काशिराजस्य दिवोदासस्य धन्वन्तरेः शिष्यः आसीत्। गुरोः समीपे सः आयुर्वेदं विशेषतः शल्यतन्त्रं च अधीतवान्। पश्चात् सः स्वयं आचार्यः भूत्वा बहून् शिष्यान् शल्यतन्त्रम् अपाठयत्। तस्य ज्ञानं 'सुश्रुतसंहिता' इति ग्रन्थे सङ्गृहीतम् अस्ति। अतः सः 'शल्यचिकित्साजनकः' इति कथ्यते।

(२) 'शल्यम्' इति शब्दस्य अर्थः — शरीरे प्रविष्टं दुःखकरं वस्तु, यथा शरः, कण्टकः, अस्थिखण्डः वा। यः वैद्यः शस्त्रेण शल्यं निष्कासयति व्रणं च चिकित्सति, सः शल्यवैद्यः। सुश्रुतः अवदत् — शल्यतन्त्रं सर्वेषु तन्त्रेषु प्रधानम्, यतः तत् शीघ्रं फलं ददाति।

(३) सुश्रुतसंहितायाम् एकोत्तरशतं (१०१) यन्त्राणि एकविंशत्यधिकशतं (१२१) शस्त्राणि च वर्णितानि। यन्त्राणि कुण्ठितानि उपकरणानि — यथा संदंशयन्त्रम्। शस्त्राणि तीक्ष्णानि — यथा वृद्धिपत्रम्। सुश्रुतः उक्तवान् — सर्वेषां यन्त्राणां हस्तः एव श्रेष्ठः, यतः हस्तं विना किमपि यन्त्रं न प्रवर्तते। बहूनि यन्त्राणि पशूनां पक्षिणां च मुखानाम् आकारेण निर्मितानि, यथा सिंहमुखं यन्त्रम्।

(४) सुश्रुतः अष्टविधानि शस्त्रकर्माणि अवर्णयत् — छेद्यं (छेदनम्), भेद्यं (भेदनम्), लेख्यं (लेखनम्), वेध्यं (वेधनम्), एष्यं (अन्वेषणम्), आहार्यम् (आहरणम्), विस्राव्यं (विस्रावणम्), सीव्यं (सीवनम्) च। नासासंधानं तस्य प्रसिद्धतमं कर्म — छिन्नायाः नासिकायाः पुनर्निर्माणं गण्डात् गृहीतेन त्वक्खण्डेन। नेत्रयोः तिमिररोगस्य (clouded lens) चिकित्सा अपि संहितायां वर्णिता। शरीरे सप्तोत्तरशतं (१०७) मर्माणि सन्ति — तानि रक्षणीयानि इति सुश्रुतः पुनः पुनः अवदत्।

(५) शिक्षणे सुश्रुतस्य पद्धतिः अद्भुता आसीत्। शिष्याः प्रथमं फलेषु शाकेषु च अभ्यासं (योग्याम्) अकुर्वन् — छेदनं कूष्माण्डे अलाबौ च, वेधनं मृतपशूनां सिरासु पद्मनाले च, एषणं घुणभक्षिते काष्ठे, सीवनं वस्त्रे मृदुचर्मणि च, बन्धनं वस्त्रनिर्मितायां पुत्तलिकायाम्। शरीरज्ञानाय सुश्रुतः शवच्छेदनम् (dissection) आवश्यकं मन्यते स्म — प्रत्यक्षेण दृष्टं ज्ञानम् एव स्थिरं भवति इति।

(६) वैद्यधर्मविषये सुश्रुतः अवदत् — वैद्यः शुचिः, दयालुः, सत्यवादी, अलुब्धः च भवेत्। सः रोगिणं पुत्रम् इव पश्येत्। रोगिणः गृहवार्तां सः कदापि बहिः न कथयेत्। शास्त्रज्ञानं कर्मकौशलं च — उभयम् अपि वैद्यस्य आवश्यकम्। सुश्रुतस्य ग्रन्थः अरबीभाषायाम् अपि अनूदितः; अद्य सर्वे देशाः तं शल्यचिकित्साजनकं मन्यन्ते।

शब्दार्थः (Word meanings)

वैद्यः = physician; न्यवसत् = lived, dwelt; शिष्यः = student, disciple; अधीतवान् = studied; अपाठयत् = taught; सङ्गृहीतम् = collected, compiled; शल्यम् = a foreign body causing pain (arrow, thorn, splinter); निष्कासयति = removes, extracts; व्रणः = wound; तीक्ष्णानि = sharp; कुण्ठितानि = blunt; संदंशयन्त्रम् = forceps (grasping instrument); हस्तः = hand; छेदनम् = excision, cutting off; भेदनम् = incision, cutting open; लेखनम् = scraping; वेधनम् = puncturing; एषणम्/अन्वेषणम् = probing; आहरणम् = extraction; विस्रावणम् = drainage (of fluids); सीवनम् = suturing, stitching; नासासंधानम् = joining/reconstruction of the nose (rhinoplasty); गण्डः = cheek; त्वक्खण्डः = piece of skin (flap); तिमिरम् = darkness; here the eye disease with clouded vision; मर्म = vital point of the body; योग्या = practical rehearsal, training exercise; कूष्माण्डः = ash gourd; अलाबुः = bottle gourd; सिरा = vein, vessel; पद्मनालम् = lotus stalk; घुणभक्षितं काष्ठम् = worm-eaten wood; पुत्तलिका = doll, mannequin; शवच्छेदनम् = dissection of a dead body; प्रत्यक्षम् = direct perception; शुचिः = clean, pure; दयालुः = compassionate; अलुब्धः = free from greed; अनूदितः = translated.

English rendering (सरलानुवादः)

(1) In ancient India there lived in the city of Varanasi a great physician named Sushruta. He dwelt on the bank of the Ganga. He was the disciple of Divodasa Dhanvantari, the king of Kashi. Under his guru he studied Ayurveda and especially Shalya-tantra (surgery). Later, becoming a teacher himself, he taught surgery to many students. His knowledge is compiled in the book called the Sushruta-Samhita. Hence he is called the 'father of surgery'. Tradition places him many centuries before the common era (often around the 7th–6th century BCE); historians debate the exact date, but his book has come down to us in Sanskrit.

(2) The word 'shalya' means a painful object lodged in the body — an arrow, a thorn, or a bone splinter. The physician who removes a shalya with instruments and treats the wound is a shalya-vaidya (surgeon). Sushruta held that Shalya-tantra is foremost among the branches of medicine because it gives quick results.

(3) The Sushruta-Samhita describes 101 yantras (blunt instruments, e.g. forceps) and 121 shastras (sharp instruments, e.g. scalpel-like blades). Sushruta declared the HAND to be the best of all yantras, for no instrument works without it. Many instruments were shaped after the mouths and beaks of animals and birds — e.g. the 'lion-mouth' (simha-mukha) forceps — a brilliant naming system that made them easy to remember and to make.

(4) THE SAMHITA'S STRUCTURE: the work has two parts — the पूर्वतन्त्रम् (Purva-tantra) with five sthanas (sections): सूत्रस्थानम् (fundamental principles, 46 chapters), निदानस्थानम् (diagnosis of diseases, 16), शारीरस्थानम् (anatomy and embryology, 10), चिकित्सास्थानम् (treatment, 40), कल्पस्थानम् (toxicology — poisons and their management, 8); and the उत्तरतन्त्रम् (Uttara-tantra, 66 chapters) on eyes, ears, nose and other specialised topics — about 186 chapters in all.

(5) FAMOUS PROCEDURES (described as history): Sushruta lists eight kinds of surgical operation (अष्टविधशस्त्रकर्माणि): chhedya (excision), bhedya (incision), lekhya (scraping), vedhya (puncturing), eshya (probing), aharya (extraction), visravya (drainage) and sivya (suturing). His most celebrated procedure is नासासंधानम् — reconstruction of a cut nose using a flap of skin taken from the cheek (गण्ड). In those days the nose was sometimes cut off as a punishment, so this operation restored both face and dignity. The Samhita also describes an ancient operation for the eye disease with clouded vision (couching — displacing the clouded lens with a fine probe called शलाका), management of fractures with splints and bandages, and suturing with threads and even the heads of large black ants for internal wounds. He mapped 107 marmas — vital points where injury is dangerous — which every surgeon had to know and protect.

(6) TRAINING (योग्या) AND ANATOMY: before touching a patient, students rehearsed each skill on models — incision on gourds (ash gourd, bottle gourd, cucumber), puncturing on the vessels of dead animals and on lotus stalks, probing on worm-eaten wood and bamboo, scraping on hides, suturing on cloth and soft leather, bandaging on stuffed cloth mannequins (पुत्तलिका), and cautery practice on soft flesh pieces. This is the world's earliest recorded system of simulation-based surgical training — the same principle modern medical colleges use today. For anatomy, Sushruta insisted on direct observation: a properly obtained dead body, wrapped and kept in still water for seven days, was then examined layer by layer by gentle brushing — because 'knowledge seen directly (प्रत्यक्ष) together with knowledge from the shastra makes understanding complete'.

(7) वैद्यधर्मः (THE PHYSICIAN'S ETHICS): In the chapter on the initiation of the student (शिष्योपनयनीयम्), the teacher administers a solemn charge: the physician must be clean (शुचिः), compassionate (दयालुः), truthful (सत्यवादी) and free of greed (अलुब्धः); he must treat the patient like his own son; he must never gossip about what he sees or hears in a patient's home; he must keep studying, for one science alone is not enough. Two authentic verses from the Sushruta-Samhita (public domain):

समदोषः समाग्निश्च समधातुमलक्रियः ।
प्रसन्नात्मेन्द्रियमनाः स्वस्थ इत्यभिधीयते ॥
शब्दार्थः: समदोषः = whose doshas are balanced; समाग्निः = whose digestive fire is balanced; समधातुमलक्रियः = whose tissues and eliminative functions are normal; प्रसन्न-आत्म-इन्द्रिय-मनाः = whose self, senses and mind are serene; स्वस्थः = healthy; इति अभिधीयते = is thus called.
Translation: He whose doshas, digestive fire, tissues and eliminations are in balance, and whose spirit, senses and mind are serene — he is called healthy. (A definition of health remarkably close to the modern idea of physical + mental well-being.)

एकं शास्त्रमधीयानो न विद्याच्छास्त्रनिश्चयम् ।
तस्माद् बहुश्रुतः शास्त्रं विजानीयाच्चिकित्सकः ॥
शब्दार्थः: एकं शास्त्रम् = one science only; अधीयानः = studying; न विद्यात् = would not know; शास्त्रनिश्चयम् = certainty of science; तस्मात् = therefore; बहुश्रुतः = widely learned; विजानीयात् = should understand; चिकित्सकः = the physician.
Translation: One who studies a single science alone cannot arrive at sure conclusions; therefore the physician should be widely read and understand his science (in the light of many disciplines).

(8) GLOBAL LEGACY (वैश्विकप्रभावः): Around the 8th century CE the Sushruta-Samhita was translated into Arabic (known by names such as 'Kitab-i-Susrud'), through which its ideas travelled to West Asia and beyond. In 1794 CE, a British magazine (the Gentleman's Magazine) published an eyewitness account of an Indian artisan rebuilding a man's nose by the traditional Indian method; this report astonished European surgeons and directly stimulated the modern rebirth of plastic surgery in Europe. Today medical historians across the world honour Sushruta as the father of surgery — and especially of plastic (reconstructive) surgery — and the Samhita as one of the earliest systematic textbooks of surgery in human history. His deeper lessons — learn by doing, respect the patient, keep the body's vital structures safe, and unite theory (शास्त्र) with practice (प्रत्यक्ष) — remain the foundation of medical education even now.

व्याकरणम् — Grammar from the lesson

(A) सन्धिः: विद्यात् + शास्त्रनिश्चयम् → विद्याच्छास्त्रनिश्चयम् (त् + श् → च्छ्, श्चुत्व-सन्धि); तस्मात् + बहुश्रुतः → तस्माद् बहुश्रुतः (त् → द्, जश्त्व); न + अस्ति → नास्ति (दीर्घसन्धिः); च + अस्ति → चास्ति; समाग्निः + च → समाग्निश्च (विसर्गसन्धिः)। सन्धिविच्छेदः (splitting) is tested often: e.g. स्वस्थ इत्यभिधीयते = स्वस्थः + इति + अभिधीयते; इत्यभिधीयते = इति + अभिधीयते (इ + अ → य्, यण्-सन्धिः)।

(B) समासः: शल्यचिकित्साजनकः = शल्यचिकित्सायाः जनकः (षष्ठीतत्पुरुषः — 'father OF surgery'); सुश्रुतसंहिता = सुश्रुतस्य संहिता (षष्ठीतत्पुरुषः); शस्त्रकर्म = शस्त्रेण कर्म (तृतीयातत्पुरुषः); नासासंधानम् = नासायाः संधानम् (षष्ठीतत्पुरुषः); अष्टविधम् = अष्ट विधाः यस्य तत् (बहुव्रीहि-flavoured compound meaning 'of eight kinds').

(C) विभक्तिः (case usage from the prose): गङ्गायाः तीरे — गङ्गायाः = षष्ठी ('of the Ganga'), तीरे = सप्तमी ('on the bank'); शस्त्रेण = तृतीया ('by/with the instrument'); शिष्येभ्यः = चतुर्थी ('to the students'); गण्डात् = पञ्चमी ('from the cheek'); वाराणसीनगरे = सप्तमी ('in the city of Varanasi'); रोगिणः गृहवार्ताम् — रोगिणः = षष्ठी, गृहवार्ताम् = द्वितीया (object).

(D) कृदन्तः: भूत्वा (भू + क्त्वा — 'having become'); गृहीत्वा (ग्रह् + क्त्वा — 'having taken'); ज्ञातुम् (ज्ञा + तुमुन् — 'to know'); छेत्तुम् (छिद् + तुमुन् — 'to cut'); सङ्गृहीतम् (सम् + ग्रह् + क्त — past participle 'compiled'); वर्णितानि (वर्ण् + क्त — 'described'); अधीयानः (अधि + इ + शानच् — present participle 'studying').

सारांशः (Summary)

Sushruta of Varanasi, disciple of Divodasa Dhanvantari, systematised surgery in the Sushruta-Samhita — 101 blunt yantras, 121 sharp shastras (with the hand as the best instrument), eight kinds of operations, rhinoplasty by cheek-flap, couching of the clouded lens, 107 marmas, fracture care and suturing. He trained students first on gourds, stalks, cloth and mannequins, taught anatomy by supervised dissection, and bound physicians to a strict ethical charge — cleanliness, compassion, truthfulness, confidentiality and lifelong study. Translated into Arabic and admired in Europe after 1794, his work earned him the title 'Father of Surgery'. This chapter presents all of this as the proud HISTORY of Indian science, in simple Sanskrit — not as medical guidance.

topics.name: सुश्रुतस्य जीवनम् — Life and Times of Sushruta
topics.description: Sushruta the ancient surgeon of Varanasi on the bank of the Ganga; his teacher Divodasa Dhanvantari, king of Kashi; his traditional date centuries before the common era; how his teaching was compiled into the Sushruta-Samhita and why he is called शल्यचिकित्साजनकः.

topics.name: सुश्रुतसंहिता — Structure and Contents of the Samhita
topics.description: The two parts of the Sushruta-Samhita — पूर्वतन्त्रम् with its five sthanas (सूत्र, निदान, शारीर, चिकित्सा, कल्प) and the उत्तरतन्त्रम् — about 186 chapters in all, with शल्यतन्त्र (surgery) as the central discipline, and the meaning of the word शल्यम्.

topics.name: यन्त्राणि शस्त्राणि च — Surgical Instruments
topics.description: The 101 blunt यन्त्र and 121 sharp शस्त्र described in the Samhita; the hand (हस्तः) as the foremost yantra; instruments named after the mouths and beaks of animals and birds such as सिंहमुखम्; and the eight kinds of operations (अष्टविधशस्त्रकर्माणि).

topics.name: प्रमुखशल्यकर्माणि — Famous Procedures in History
topics.description: Historic procedures described in the Samhita: नासासंधानम् (rhinoplasty with a cheek-skin flap), the ancient couching operation for clouded vision using the शलाका, suturing (सीवनम्) with threads and ant-heads, fracture care with splints, and the 107 मर्म vital points — presented as history of science, not medical advice.

topics.name: शिक्षणपद्धतिः शरीरज्ञानं च — Training Methods and Anatomy
topics.description: Sushruta's simulation-based training (योग्या): incision practised on gourds, puncturing on lotus stalks and vessels of dead animals, probing on worm-eaten wood, suturing on cloth and leather, bandaging on mannequins; and anatomy learnt by supervised dissection (शवच्छेदनम्) after a seven-day water preparation — theory united with direct observation (प्रत्यक्ष).

topics.name: वैद्यधर्मः वैश्विकप्रभावश्च — Physician Ethics and Global Legacy
topics.description: The physician's ethical charge in the शिष्योपनयनीय chapter — cleanliness, compassion, truthfulness, freedom from greed, treating the patient like a son, confidentiality, lifelong study — with authentic verses; and the world legacy: Arabic translation (Kitab-i-Susrud), the 1794 rhinoplasty report that inspired European plastic surgery, and Sushruta's title 'Father of Surgery'.

sections.heading: Sushruta of Varanasi — life and title
bullets: Sushruta was an ancient surgeon-teacher of वाराणसी (Kashi) who lived and taught on the bank of the Ganga; tradition places him many centuries BCE, though historians debate the exact date.
He learnt Ayurveda, and especially शल्यतन्त्रम् (surgery), from Divodasa Dhanvantari, the physician-king of Kashi, and later taught many disciples himself.
His teaching survives as the सुश्रुतसंहिता, one of the earliest systematic textbooks of surgery in human history — hence his title शल्यचिकित्साजनकः, 'father of surgery'.
शल्यम् means a painful foreign body (arrow, thorn, splinter); the surgeon (शल्यवैद्यः) removes it and heals the wound, which is why the discipline is called शल्यतन्त्रम्.

sections.heading: The Sushruta-Samhita — structure and contents
bullets: The Samhita has two parts: the पूर्वतन्त्रम् (five sthanas) and the उत्तरतन्त्रम् (66 chapters) — about 186 chapters altogether, in Sanskrit.
The five sthanas are सूत्रस्थानम् (principles, 46), निदानस्थानम् (diagnosis, 16), शारीरस्थानम् (anatomy-embryology, 10), चिकित्सास्थानम् (treatment, 40) and कल्पस्थानम् (toxicology, 8).
Sushruta held शल्यतन्त्र to be foremost among the branches of medicine because it acts quickly and visibly.
The उत्तरतन्त्रम् adds specialised subjects including diseases of the eye, ear and nose.

sections.heading: Instruments and the eight operations
bullets: The Samhita describes 101 यन्त्र (blunt instruments, e.g. the संदंश forceps) and 121 शस्त्र (sharp cutting instruments).
The hand (हस्तः) is declared the foremost yantra, since no instrument works without it.
Many instruments are named after the mouths and beaks of animals and birds (e.g. सिंहमुखम्, 'lion-mouth'), a memorable design-and-naming system.
Eight kinds of operation (अष्टविधशस्त्रकर्माणि) are listed: छेद्य excision, भेद्य incision, लेख्य scraping, वेध्य puncturing, एष्य probing, आहार्य extraction, विस्राव्य drainage, सीव्य suturing.

sections.heading: Famous procedures — history, not medical advice
bullets: नासासंधानम् (rhinoplasty): a cut nose was rebuilt with a flap of skin taken from the cheek (गण्ड) — the most celebrated procedure of the Samhita, restoring both face and dignity.
An ancient couching operation for clouded vision displaced the clouded lens with a fine probe (शलाका) — described purely as history of science.
Suturing (सीवनम्) used threads of plant fibre and hair, and even heads of large black ants for internal wounds; fractures were managed with splints and bandages.
Sushruta mapped 107 मर्म (vital points) where injury is dangerous; the surgeon had to know and protect them all.

sections.heading: Training, anatomy, ethics and legacy
bullets: योग्या (rehearsal): students practised incision on gourds, puncturing on lotus stalks and vessels of dead animals, probing on worm-eaten wood, suturing on cloth and soft leather, and bandaging on stuffed mannequins — the earliest recorded simulation training.
Anatomy was learnt by supervised dissection: a body kept in still water for seven days was examined layer by layer, uniting शास्त्र (theory) with प्रत्यक्ष (direct observation).

The physician's charge: be clean, compassionate, truthful and free of greed; treat the patient like a son; never reveal a patient's household matters; keep studying — एकं शास्त्रम् अधीयानः cannot reach certainty.

Legacy: translated into Arabic (Kitab-i-Susrud) around the 8th century CE; the 1794 Gentleman's Magazine account of Indian rhinoplasty inspired the rebirth of European plastic surgery; the world honours Sushruta as father of surgery.

key_takeaways: Sushruta, the ancient surgeon of Varanasi and disciple of Divodasa Dhanvantari, is honoured as शल्यचिकित्साजनकः — the father of surgery.
His सुश्रुतसंहिता (Purva-tantra of five sthanas + Uttara-tantra, about 186 chapters) is one of the earliest systematic surgery textbooks in the world.
It describes 101 blunt यन्त्र and 121 sharp शस्त्र — with the hand declared the foremost instrument — and eight kinds of operations.
नासासंधानम्, rebuilding a cut nose with a cheek-skin flap, is his most celebrated procedure and the ancestor of modern plastic surgery.
Students trained first on gourds, stalks, cloth and mannequins (योग्या), and learnt anatomy by supervised dissection — theory (शास्त्र) united with direct observation (प्रत्यक्ष).
Sushruta bound physicians to strict ethics: cleanliness, compassion, truthfulness, freedom from greed, confidentiality, and lifelong wide study.
Through the Arabic Kitab-i-Susrud and the 1794 report that amazed Europe, Sushruta's legacy became global — and this chapter studies it as history of Indian science, not as medical advice.
